column2: A note indicates that Duncan may have heard the lecture (Olson's) on a visit to BMC in the late 1940s.

During his stay in the summer of 1948, Cage performs only Satie's work and precedes the concerts with a speech denouncing Beethoven's harmonic tradition in favor of Satie's emphasis on rhythm and duration, which exasperates the German émigrés, Albers included. An all-Satie program; an introductory speech Consequences: The later break in the Cage-Albers friendship over chance

An innovative production of Satie's play, until then performed once and then ignored. The student Arthur Penn directs: Buckminster Fuller as Baron Medusa, Elaine de Kooning as his daughter Frisette, Merce Cunningham as the “costly mechanical monkey,” sets by Bill and Elaine de Kooning. An avant-garde theater style: deliberately non-naturalistic, stylized acting, no boundary between stage space and audience. Photographed by Clemens Kalischer. Specific roles; sets by the de Koonings; Satie's absurd monologues and unrelated musical interludes Consequences: Redeems Cage's position at the college; prepares the ground for arbitrary links between the events of a production

A major summer session: Willem and Elaine de Kooning teach (BMC 1948), as do Cage and Cunningham; Fuller gives his course (photographed by Beaumont Newhall with Elaine de Kooning in the class); Lippold prepares Devotion I; and Satie's play The Ruse of Medusa is staged, directed by Arthur Penn with Cunningham and Fuller, sets by Elaine and Willem de Kooning, photographed by Clemens Kalischer. Cage photographed at the piano in 1948 by Kalischer; Cunningham photographed teaching

In the privacy of her student studio, she tears out a page of her diary on which she had written her feelings of the moment and reassembles it into an illegible collage titled Secrets: by cutting up the words and putting them back together at random, she conceals her private thoughts. a torn diary page, words reassembled into a disordered pattern Consequences: words begin to enter her art; she sees in it the origin of her taste for fragmentation and unexpected juxtaposition

The “original Happening”: Cage's production with a stepladder, radio, dogs, and dancers, in the summer of 1948 — Cage created it, says Dawson, the way one must create Black Mountain in order to write it. a stepladder, radios, dogs, dancers

According to George Butterick's introduction, the ambitious Olson sent the three sections to the New Yorker, which returned them within eight days, as they do. Returned within a week Consequences: Freed from magazine ambitions, he was able to follow Dahlberg and go to lecture on Melville

Encouraged by Dahlberg, Olson accepts the invitation and comes to Black Mountain to lecture on Melville: he takes a step into his future, leaves behind the worry of being “a writer,” goes through this experience, and comes out of it a poet. Consequences: Olson will become a central figure and then rector of the college

During a Satie play staged in the dining hall for lack of curtains, the set pieces were covered with newspapers, removed just before the start. Albers, sitting beside Ray in the audience, told Ray it was better with the newspapers. Newspapers whisked away just before the action; no curtains; the dining hall as theater Consequences: Ray Spillenger, decades later in his kitchen, a scotch and ice water in hand, weeps as he tells it: he was right!

That summer, after a conversation with de Kooning, Joe Fiore decided to go on as an artist rather than as a musician. His father was a violinist in the Cleveland Orchestra under George Szell. A father who played violin under George Szell

Friends gladly leave their society without community to found an invented community where at least their naked hatred can be expressed; they choose a pleasant place with a waterfall, a pond reflecting the sky, vegetation, and animals, but are paralyzed by the anguish of justifying their city's existence. a foaming waterfall plunging into a flat pool that reflects the blue sky; a dark fire that flares into visibility on the faces; Mynheer's heart changed into a small paving stone; notes scribbled on the back of a marriage certificate Consequences: a dilemma: to name themselves a community or not to live at all

Mynheer calculates the roles needed to form a child's personality: a nurse, a bad rival mother (the aunt type), a good rival mother (the big-sister type), a neutral older woman, 3-4 fathers (the uncle type), an older brother to be avoided, a favorite younger brother (the Abel type), a sexual friend, a nonsexual rival friend, an object of disinterested devotion, a gang of 2-3 males, an outside scapegoat, a sexually active older girlfriend, a younger girlfriend, a maniac, a dying old man, a stranger bearing infinite mystery — 22 in all. With a safety factor of 3 (since before three people the soul favors one, disfavors one, and allies itself with one), and each person able to play several roles, the community requires 66 people, a suburban community heavily weighted toward children. 22 roles × a factor of 3 = 66 people; a few animals would also be needed for the continuity of the species, and perhaps an Angel Consequences: the target community is modest in size, suburban

Mynheer proposes, on the model of Remus killed by his brother to give Rome a beginning, to sacrifice a member of the group and plow his crushed skull into the field: the dead man would justify the city. Silence, hostile looks; Droyt furiously asks why his father exempts himself; Horatio, in tears, recalls Raymond, his only friend, killed in the days of the Grand Piano, his chosen father and Arthur, dead in the war, and refuses to lose Piet Duyck — he begins to howl frightfully; Minetta wittily turns the situation around: dead, she would haunt the city forever, and they would never be rid of her; people laugh, baring their teeth. Mynheer licks his lips, weighs the black stone that fills his palm, raises his forearm to throw it; everyone draws back, shouting Consequences: no sacrifice carried out; the tension rises

A tall redhead unknown to everyone, refusing to give his name or the friend who sent him, introduces himself as the third displaced person of Harry Tyler's joke (South Africa — so far from what?), come to fill the role of the Stranger. He explains that he changes masks every other day so as to stay mysterious to the children; he shows a mask under which his red hair can be seen; he denies being a Jew (the Jew is the Outside, the Scapegoat; he is the Stranger); he reels off a routine with interlaced fingers about numbers (22, 33, 55, 66). In the evening, drunk, he turns sinister: community seekers, death cowards, he calls them, and he refuses to leave when asked. a mask brought in his pocket; he has drunk a great deal; “Nobody invited you. Why don't you go away?” — “Hell, I'll go away! Can you make me?” Consequences: he clings on where he does not belong, fulfilling his role

In the darkness, a face lit by a flashlight, a bell rings: each person utters his naked hatred — of children who imprison, of unsatisfied sexual demands, of friends who choose the wrong moment, of desirable strangers who do not respond, of one's own cowardly self, of poor clothes, of those who crunch apples too loudly, of those who beat children, of the order of the world. The narrator adds that he hates his poetic art, because to be its poet he has had to be himself and lead the miserable life he leads. The bell strikes twelve; an appeal is made to the Creator Spirit, the only meaning of a universe that otherwise does not seriously recommend itself. eyes narrowed to slits, a jutting jaw; a flashlight trained; a bell striking twelve Consequences: the community is at last founded on the shared avowal of hatred

After the declarations of hatred, someone proposes putting out the lights and sleeping. Mynheer declares that there is enough hatred to cement “community relations”. Each gives a last thought: Lothair takes apart the illusion of the man of simple desires; the dancer Rosalind mocks the artist who weeps over the life sacrificed to the work. the first to fall asleep is the professional Stranger, who snores confidently; Rosalind falls asleep in the middle of the narrator's protest Consequences: the community exists, there is no need to prove it; fully formed personalities (mothers, fathers, teachers, seducers, scapegoats)

In the fall of 1948, Elaine de Kooning reads Kierkegaard, a precursor of existentialism, to her husband Bill; she perceives an affinity between Bill's taste for stubborn perseverance and Kierkegaard's exaltation of it, and between Bill and K.'s ordinary heroes. Consequences: Kierkegaard becomes an intimate reference for the painter; he will later reuse the title Fear and Trembling
Pat Passlof studies with de Kooning in 1948; she will testify in 1989 in Art Journal.

In his first summer at Black Mountain, Fuller tries unsuccessfully to assemble a geodesic dome. Geodesics defined as arcs of great circles Consequences: He recovers thanks to the student Kenneth Snelson's innovations in “tensegrity”

The sculpture student Kenneth Snelson's innovations in “tensegrity” (discontinuous compression, continuous tension) redirect Fuller away from his “energetic geometry”. Discontinuous compression and continuous tension; physical models of close-packed spheres Consequences: The geodesic dome, prototyped with tensegrity, becomes the matrix of Fuller's holistic plan
A silver print of Cage at the college in 1948 by Kalischer. gelatin silver print

In the late 1940s, Cage meets resistance as a composer (less as a performer on the prepared piano). Albers offers him a teaching post for the 1948 summer session — his first post in musical composition. Cage is delighted. the prepared piano: objects inserted between the strings, percussive playing Consequences: Cage's first teaching of composition

Cage plays only Satie's work all summer instead of giving an overview of modern music in general; an introductory speech denouncing Beethoven's harmonic tradition in favor of rhythm and duration in Satie particularly angers the German émigrés. Consequences: A lasting resentment of Cage at the college

A universally admired production of Satie's long-neglected play, translated that summer by Mary Caroline Richards. Arthur Penn directs: Fuller plays Baron Medusa, Elaine de Kooning his daughter Frisette, Cunningham the mechanical monkey Jonas. Sets and props by Fuller, Willem and Elaine de Kooning, and the students Ruth Asawa and Ray Johnson. props: a velvet footstool with giant human feet, a monumental thermometer topped with an outsized paper bow, the baron's desk painted in trompe-l'œil using a secret guild technique that Elaine de Kooning says he learned as a teenager in Holland, surrounded by enormous four-sided triangles around its feet (a nod to Fuller's tetrahedrons) Consequences: Revives the college's tradition of experimental theater, dormant since Schawinsky's departure in 1938

In his first summer at Black Mountain, Cage remembers that he saw eye to eye with Albers and that their conversations were marked by agreement, despite a generation's difference in age. Consequences: As soon as Cage introduces chance into his practice, they will be permanently at odds

While working on Boulez's Second Piano Sonata (1948), Tudor admits to Richards that his difficulties are not with the notes but with the music; to understand it, he reads Boulez's sources: Mallarmé and Artaud. Tudor's remark: he had no problems with the notes, but with the music. Consequences: It is through Tudor that Richards discovers Artaud.

In the summer of 1948 Fuller teaches a course he titles for the first time “comprehensive design”; he then refines there his conception of experimentation as a test aimed at entirely rethinking postwar technocratic society. he writes the phrase for the first time as the title of the course Consequences: A third model of experimentation at the college, after Albers and Cage

Fuller coins the phrase “comprehensive design” as the title of the course he teaches at the college during the 1948 summer session; he then refines it during his summers at Black Mountain Consequences: The phrase becomes the heart of his theory of experimentation as total design

Albers invites Fuller to teach at the 1948 summer session; Fuller is a last-minute substitute for the Harvard architect Bertrand Goldberg, a former Bauhaus student, the faculty having received several refusals from candidates who were too busy Consequences: The start of two decisive summers for Fuller and for the college's rhetoric of experimentation

A Fortune article in the spring of 1948 reveals the collapse of the Wichita House's mass-production plans; Black Mountain's invitation follows closely on this publication Consequences: Fuller arrives at the college in the full notoriety of failure

A profile of Fuller proposed for Science Illustrated prompts internal requests to include the reasons for the failures of his projects and why he never carries things through Consequences: An illustration of Fuller's discredit on the eve of Black Mountain

Fuller accepts his very first teaching commission in the summer of 1948, a refuge at a time when his career is beset by setbacks and criticism. Consequences: The beginning of his involvement with the college and of his relationship to teaching.
On his arrival in 1948, Fuller meets the sculpture student Kenneth Snelson, who is fired up by the new instructor's ideas. Consequences: A collaboration that leads to tensegrity.

Every morning in the summer of 1948, Fuller, Cage, and Cunningham have breakfast together outdoors under the trees and playfully work out the scheme of a “finishing school”: a caravan school traveling from town to town, which would “finish” everything — that is, break up all conventional approaches to school. a daily breakfast outdoors under the trees Consequences: A shared formulation of a model of the test as an act of radical transformation, opposed to Albers's systematic method.

A largely Germanic school: Cage's devotion to Satie irritates. Albers, to calm things down, requires Cage to give a talk before each concert. In the middle of the session, Cage gives a lecture longer than the others in which, to set out Satie's anti-Beethoven views, he denounces Beethoven: the effect was like a bomb falling on the place. Consequences: A memorable tension between Cage and the college's German musical culture

Fuller's first attempt to assemble a geodesic dome at the college fails; it is then that he is said to have uttered the reported phrase (see quotations). Consequences: Fuller perseveres and returns in the summer of 1949 with reinforced materials (known from other sources).

A summer course in 1948 at the college, a revised version at the Institute of Design from October 4, 1948, to January 29, 1949; the synopsis becomes the essay “Comprehensive Designing” (1963). A synopsis dated “Oct. 4, '48 – Jan. 29, '49,” pp. 1-1h, Fuller Papers. Consequences: The method of comprehensive design enters the college.

Hansgirg suggests acquiring two of Fuller's structures (Wichita/Dymaxion houses) for the campus, after the Fortune article of May 1948, “What Became of the Fuller House”. Consequences: A project not carried out (domes built instead).

According to Snelson, Fuller arrives for the 1948 summer session as a replacement for an architecture teacher who withdrew at the last minute; it is his first teaching post. Consequences: The beginning of the Fuller-Snelson relationship and of the legendary summer of 1948 (Cage, Cunningham, de Kooning…).

According to the sculpture student Kenneth Snelson, Fuller arrives for the summer session as a replacement for an architecture teacher who withdrew at the last minute; it is his first teaching post. Consequences: A decisive meeting with Snelson and Elaine de Kooning

Five years after her marriage to Willem de Kooning, Elaine begins publishing regularly in ARTnews, where Thomas Hess will be editor. Consequences: She contributes actively to her husband's reputation and to the couple's public image.
The exhibition of black-and-white paintings establishes de Kooning's preeminence as an abstract painter. Consequences: Consolidates him as a major figure of the New York avant-garde

Elaine tells Renee Arb, who was reviewing Bill's first solo exhibition at the Egan Gallery, that Art News criticism is amateurish, written by art historians who know nothing about art. Renee repeats the remark to Tom Hess, who replies: “Tell her to come in and see me”. When she comes by the office, he gives her five exhibitions; four artists strike her as mediocre or dreadful, the fifth is Alberto Giacometti, on whom she writes a passionate and authoritative review: the exhibition seems the output of a civilization rather than the work of a single man. Bill, overwhelmed, leaves the gallery, walks around the block to calm down, then comes back to study the work more closely. Hess hires her as an editorial associate and hands her a list of twenty exhibitions to review for the month's issue. Five exhibitions, then twenty; the magazine's policy: situate the artist, describe the work, judge it; the rate: 2 dollars per review, whether two sentences or two hundred words. Consequences: The start of a regular career as an art critic; the founding Giacometti review.

In 1948, at the innovative college of Black Mountain, Elaine paints her Black Mountain series, in which Arshile Gorky's inspiration on her painting is at its deepest. Consequences: The Black Mountain series becomes a major body of her work.
1948 is the year Rothko enters his Present: his earlier work no longer represents him as he is known from then on. Consequences: The beginning of the classic period of the large rectangular canvases.

Pollock makes unpleasant remarks to Gorky about his painting; Gorky, smiling dangerously, takes a pencil from one pocket and a penknife from the other and, without taking his eyes off Pollock, slowly sharpens the point against his thumb. Gorky's retort: “Pardon me, Mr. Pollock, you and I are different kinds of artists”; Pollock, swaying a little, answers with a sly, approving little smile and turns away, satisfied

In the spring of 1948, Greenberg gives a cocktail party to introduce Leo Castelli to American artists: Gorky, Pollock, Smith, Kline, de Kooning — the five future subjects of “Strokes of Genius”. Consequences: A symbolic gathering of the five artists of the future series

Two weeks after Christmas, the temperature drops sharply and the lake freezes; everyone slides and pulls sleds; the nursery group is pulled around on chairs and washtubs; Natasha Goldowsky, a former ballet dancer turned physicist, an exuberant star. Skates taken in turn.

Hess takes over the direction of Art News, trying to appear neutral in the de Kooning–Pollock rivalry, which his affair with Elaine and her hiring compromise. Consequences: Elaine joins the Art News staff

After a party that is too noisy, Bill draws Elaine out onto a country road; the absolute silence and the vault of stars overwhelm him; he breaks the quiet and wants to go back. Words: Bill wants to go back to the party; the universe gives him the creeps. Atmosphere: total darkness, silence, a dome of stars Stakes: Revealing the fear of the void beneath the reveler's mask; shedding light on the giant star in Woman.

After three months, Frankfurter, still doubtful, accuses her of writing only favorable reviews; she retorts: “That's disgusting, isn't it,” and walks out of the office Words: “That's disgusting, isn't it”; on favoritism: they were all her friends; she knows everyone; no favoritism possible Atmosphere: a curt confrontation, a theatrical exit Stakes: her conception of criticism against editorial authority

During the Satie Festival, diners stand up and proclaim their positions on the very existence of music; the community splits into two camps for the whole summer Atmosphere: Electricity, excitement, quarrel Stakes: An aesthetic battle for the soul of the college

One or two very noisy, merry tables; at each, two or three stiff, silent diners; the non-mush line snakes toward the kitchen, served by the cooks; a few conscientious souls carry their plates over to the mushers to win converts. Atmosphere: A theater of ideologies at a fixed hour, trays as flags. Stakes: The community discovers live that it is not unanimous — and that unanimity cannot be decreed.

A proposal for a collective sacrifice for European relief; speeches on moral responsibility and universal guilt; a chain of zealous suggestions; Rondthaler proposes giving up smoking; voices suggest he give up milk instead; the final motion: a weekly mush, adopted by acclamation, the meeting adjourned; the half-dissents, barely articulated, remain in the room. Words: Let Rondthaler give up milk instead of tobacco; speeches on universal guilt toward the persecuted. Atmosphere: A wave of moral fervor that makes rational objection impossible. Stakes: Utopia trips over its own virtue: the good by decree becomes an ultimatum.

Penn, worried that no one will come to the tryouts, insists to his roommate; Stiles reads Saroyan and gets a part in the Stein Words: Penn on Liliom: his reading is “hammy,” but he will straighten him out. Atmosphere: roommate complicity, the young director's anxiety Stakes: launching the theater project

On a bench, the blonde wonders what it is like to be a queen; two kings arrive with paper crowns and cardboard axes and invite her to choose; she laughs at them; they kill each other; she sits up, head held high: kings are useless Words: “I am Phillip Hall, and that is all” / “All you have to do is to be first, and then you are a King” / “I am a Queen; I can tell by feeling. It is so lovely to be a Queen.” Atmosphere: a children's game, a triumph “with brilliance” Stakes: Stiles's only triumph as an actor

After the empty exhibition, a letter from a stranger — Albers, whose name means nothing to them but the Bauhaus — offers $200, board, the train for two, and a studio each; they draw up a budget: $70 for Bill's studio, $36 for the flat, $94 left over; elation. Atmosphere: From despair to euphoria: all their problems were solved Stakes: The invitation that changes an artistic trajectory

An hour and a half of fruitless fiddling by the engineers; Bill comes in, weighs, studies, and snaps the two pieces together: a perfect cube. Fuller nods, not surprised. Words: Bill later: he looked for the least logical way Atmosphere: amused astonishment Stakes: The artist's intuition against the engineers' logic

A rainy day; the whole school comes to sneer; the fully assembled dome stays slumped on the grass; yet everyone knows it is theoretically brilliant. Words: Bucky: let's put it together anyway; “One never knows the ways of the Almighty.” Atmosphere: rain, collective derision, Fuller's faith intact Stakes: The public failure of a brilliant idea

Many rehearsals are needed to keep from bursting out laughing at Fuller's antics; Penn draws characters out of total amateurs; the making of the gauze dress and Bucky's costume. Atmosphere: helpless laughter, craftsmanship, collective creativity Stakes: An engineering genius revealed as a comic actor

Albers approaches Bill at the end of the summer: ten students, six are leaving for New York in September, does he know anything about it? Bill answers bluntly that he told them to leave school, take a studio, and paint Words: Albers: he had ten students; six are leaving the college for New York in September; does he know anything about it? Bill: of course; he told them that if they wanted to be artists, they had to leave school, come to New York, take a studio, and start painting. Atmosphere: tense, then relaxed; Albers does not seem to take it badly Stakes: two conceptions of an artist's training; an omen of the future (Yale)

The treasurer's table; Bobby teases Oates about his Chinese painting and suggests the ascetic painter of misty mountains; Oates's answer makes Mark get up, walk around the table, and kiss him Words: Bobby, gently mocking, suggests he go into the mountains and paint misty landscapes as an ascetic Atmosphere: a warm welcome, the newcomer's emotion Stakes: anything can happen here, and he can be part of it

Bill, disgusted with the crowd, proposes a walk; ten minutes later no light from the college can be seen; velvety darkness, an almost terrifying silence, a multitude of stars; then Bill wants to go back Words: Bill: let's go back to the party; the universe gives him the creeps. Atmosphere: starry immensity, cosmic dread Stakes: the painter facing the void

Students set out to tan a whole hide from the farm with a manual but without the ingredients or the tools; every day the smell gets worse; they scrape valiantly; the hide is never playable and ends up as a prop in a skit Atmosphere: An increasingly powerful, nauseating smell; the plucky diligence of the little group Stakes: Craft enthusiasm against recalcitrant matter

During the dance numbers, a crew runs the slackened drums to the kitchen, holds them over the ranges, taps them, hears the note rise, and brings the instrument back for the next number — the unsung heroes of the program Atmosphere: Running, the heat of the ranges, little plinks of sound Stakes: The show goes on thanks to invisible logistics

Fuller grabs Davidoff in the corridor, pulls her into a dark closet, and eagerly points to a material that glows in the dark; he would have grabbed the first person who came along to share his discovery Words: She simply has to come and see something Atmosphere: Darkness, absolute childlike joy

After Cage's anti-Beethoven provocations, Bodky gently strikes back at a party with a rather witty Satie pastiche at the piano Atmosphere: A party atmosphere, an elegant riposte Stakes: The Beethoven/Satie aesthetic war in a minor key

A student asks de Kooning what he thinks about while painting; he points to a canvas and explains that it comes from the sight of a woman's heel in an open shoe, seen from behind: the flesh of the heel spilling over the edges of the sole

Penn posts the announcement of an acting class twice a week; he expects few people and sees twenty to thirty turn up, including the three teachers with whom he is himself studying. Words: Penn: “I just simply didn't know very much... I really hadn't read properly almost anything” Atmosphere: Astonishment and collective enthusiasm Stakes: A 24-year-old student becomes the teacher of his own teachers

The conflict over repeating the plays is played out in class; an initial vote of 11 for, 1 against — the stubborn opponent holds the lead role; Wallen sets the task: work out a course of action that satisfies the one as much as the eleven; the class shifts the debate and invents the demonstration performance; Wallen warns against imposing the solution on the rest of the troupe; the cast adopts a modified version. Words: Actors: “We've given the plays already... we work for ourselves” Atmosphere: Tension, then inventiveness and collective relief Stakes: Consensus at eleven to one: community democracy put to the test by a single man

The hostile version: Penn deliberately fosters a fragile student's love for him to deepen her acting, then bids her a cold farewell after the last performance — she comes close to a breakdown. The favorable version: before him, she was only a nebbish, a quivering protoplasm, and acting made her blossom; Penn merely acted as a good director should. Words: Penn's defender: she “blossomed into a beautiful human being” Atmosphere: Rumors, camps, a reputation at stake Stakes: The psychological price of the Stanislavsky method applied to amateurs

The students denounce the project as a barracks or a beach house, dispute its functionalism, demand small dormitories of ten to fourteen people, and present their own plans. Words: The building denounced as fitter for a barracks or a beach house than for a dormitory, at odds with Black Mountain's known aversion to mass affairs. Atmosphere: Controversy, commitment. Stakes: Testing the students' real power against the Board and the teachers.

Lippold, turned down for lack of money and housing, writes that he has bought an old hearse: transport for his wife and two children, a dormitory on the spot, in exchange for the college's plumbing; he offers a talk on Rilke. Cage adds his own bid by night letter: the hearse has been tested for sleeping. Words: Cage: they have tested their hearse for sleeping, and it works; he has not mentioned all the many others who also want to come Atmosphere: Tragicomic, the cheerful poverty of New York artists Stakes: Getting a penniless family admitted to a penniless college

Two weeks after his arrival, Droll, in sandals and rolled-up khakis, begins to understand the conversations — until the night when Fuller explains to him that by standing a certain way one can feel the earth move. Words: Fuller: if you stand a certain way, you can feel the earth turning Atmosphere: A starry night, the vertigo of conversion Stakes: The intimate turning point of a boy fresh from military academy

At lunch, Levi taps his glass; very seriously, he announces an insoluble split in the faculty and proposes, as rector, a duel to the death: the Beethovenians armed with cold Wiener schnitzels, the Satieists with flaming crêpes Suzette, in the kitchen. A general food fight breaks out. Words: Levi declares that only unprecedented means can resolve an unprecedented crisis Atmosphere: Levi's imperturbable seriousness, helpless laughter, flying food Stakes: Defusing the Cage/Bodky quarrel through absurdity

At the open rehearsals, heavily attended that day, Fuller confesses to Penn his fear of making a fool of himself. Penn improvises a series of exercises in which the two of them hop about, laugh artificially, and roll on the floor; the exercise becomes fun, then liberating, then inventive; Fuller blossoms. Words: Fuller: he is afraid of making a silly fool of himself Atmosphere: Initial embarrassment, joyful madness, liberation Stakes: A psychological lever: making Fuller feel that ridicule is not fatal

He asks each person what he read over the summer; each title is condemned as read at eighteen, twenty-one, or twenty-four and now recognized as terrible. Martha says she read all of Proust because it was there. Later, during an oral report on Madame Bovary in which she regrets that Emma married out of carnal lust, he shoots back at once. Words: “My dear Miss Rittenhouse, for what reasons do you intend to marry?” Atmosphere: Provocation, mutual insolence, a war of respectabilities Stakes: Who dominates the class: the master or the students

Every evening, leftover paint flung with a trowel onto the canvas in Hebei's room; at the end of the year, the canvas covered, signed “Anonymous Blotch,” hung up; some examine it gravely, Bolotowsky identifies each palette and laughs, the dupes feel humiliated, and Bolotowsky makes it a theoretical defense of chance to enrage Albers. Words: Bolotowsky: “He started it and I kept it up” Atmosphere: A studio prank, the unease of the duped spectators Stakes: The joke as a weapon in the war over “standards”

Less than two weeks after his arrival, Dahlberg declares that he cannot take any more; Albers, very kind, begs him to stay; inwardly he refuses — let the students defy one another, he is leaving — and leaves the same day. He will get Olson as his replacement. Words: “Albers was very kind and beseeched me to remain” Atmosphere: Exhaustion, courteous irritation Stakes: The college loses its literature teacher — and gains Olson

Two nonartist students found sleeping together one night in the Studies Building; Albers seeks to expel them; the girl threatens to post a medical certificate attesting that she is virgo intacta; the two end up staying. Atmosphere: A sexual scandal, a duel of authority and absurdity Stakes: Albers's moral authority contested

The Lippold family arrives in an old black hearse; Fuller, delighted, praises its classical columns and big windows; Richards lends a dime for the children's ice cream. Words: Fuller: “a beautiful old motor hearse… Beautiful black classical columns and great glass windows” Atmosphere: Poor but cheerful, mutual help, bohemian folklore Stakes: The college's poverty at the very moment its most famous summer arrives (Cage, Cunningham, Fuller)

Cage declares at table that Beethoven was wrong and that his influence has been deadly for music; he contrasts Satie and Webern, who structure by durations; Bodky, indignant, speaks of desecration; the dispute becomes a verbal duel. Words: Cage: “Beethoven was in error”… he ran music aground on an island of decadence; Bodky sees it as a “desecration” Atmosphere: sudden tension around the table, the anger of a man of traditional music Stakes: the old musical world against the avant-garde, in the presence of the students

During the exhibition, Elaine and Egan beam together at the bar; Bill, hunched over a drink, turns his back on them and shrugs, as he always did with Elaine's lovers and with the women who left him. Atmosphere: smoke, an ostentatious indifference visible to all Stakes: the couple's wager: infidelity as a strategy for fame

When her mockery of the Art News reviews is reported to him, Hess, half amused and half serious, asks her whether she thinks she can do better; without a second's hesitation, she takes up the challenge. Words: reviews written by art history students who have never looked at anything Atmosphere: provocation and self-assurance Stakes: Elaine enters the critical establishment

A very boozy party; Betsy, jealous of everything about Elaine, challenges her to arm wrestling; elbows squarely on the table, hands clasped; much grunting and puffing; a draw; the two women fall into a friendly love with each other. Words: Elaine attacks laughing, “roaring into battle” Atmosphere: collective drunkenness, an audience of betting artists, a comic turn into reconciliation Stakes: marital jealousy turned into complicity

Goodman lectures on Kafka before an audience of students, mostly veterans financed by the G.I. Bill; the audience protests frantically that Kafka is psychotic and has no connection with reality; Goodman notes the irony: these men lived through part of The Trial and are at that very moment wandering beneath The Castle. Words: The students: Kafka is psychotic, one should pay no attention to him, he has no connection with reality. Atmosphere: Tension, the defensive disbelief of a generation in shock from the war and the bomb Stakes: Youth refuses the literature that describes it; the birth of the apathy of the 1950s

The first day of art class. Susan, shy, is drawing. Kurzen hands her a piece of charcoal, suggests that she feel the edges of the sheet, close her eyes, and draw a rooster filling the whole page. She does so and feels the joy of creating by following the mind's eye. Words: Kurzen suggests she feel the edges of the paper, close her eyes, and draw a rooster filling the entire page. Atmosphere: The intimacy of the gesture, confidence passed on by the teacher, a sudden clearing Stakes: The birth of a vocation: the shy student becomes a painter in an instant.

At the height of the governance crisis, the summer institute organized by Albers brings together Cage, Cunningham, de Kooning, and Fuller; people crowd onto the porch for the photo; Albers confides to Lippold his weariness of the annual cycle: every year a new crowd thinks it will change everything, stability returns at the end, and then it all starts again. Words: Albers to Lippold: every year “a whole bunch of people come and think they're going to change it all” Atmosphere: Creative ferment against the exhaustion of the pioneers Stakes: The artistic peak coincides with Albers's weariness

Tworkov writes his sister and brother-in-law a long letter describing the freedom of the place: everyone studies or idles as he pleases, comes up for examination when he wants, professors meet classes as they please; and yet a great deal of work gets done, with a quality of good manners that is gentle and sweet. Words: Tworkov's letter: the greatest freedom to be what one wants to be… there is simply no pattern of behavior Atmosphere: summer freedom, superb mountains, intellectual permissiveness Stakes: utopia lived at the very moment the internal struggles begin

A performance of Satie's play with an all-star cast; Clemens Kalischer photographs it (an 11 x 14-inch gelatin silver print, Asheville Art Museum). Stakes: The convergence of the European avant-garde and the Americans

Albers asks Cage to justify Satie's importance before a musical community of Germanic allegiance. Cage delivers a disguised manifesto: only one new idea since Beethoven, that of Webern and Satie — the parts defined by length in time and not by harmony. He accuses Beethoven of having killed the art of music. According to legend, Paul Goodman walks out furious; Duberman establishes that he was not there that summer. Words: Cage: there has been only one new idea since Beethoven… in Webern and Satie; Beethoven responsible for a “deadening of the art of music”. Atmosphere: A polemical evening, a theoretical thunderclap in a community attached to the German tradition. Stakes: A clash of two conceptions of music — and of community — on the college's own ground.

Fuller tries to raise his first geodesic dome during the summer session; mixed results; the following summer, the students raise it successfully and enthusiastically at his side. Atmosphere: Humility, then collective exaltation Stakes: Experimentation as teaching: failure accepted, a rebound

During the 1948 summer session, the director of industrial design at MoMA offers Albers a solo exhibition; she devotes herself to it from the fall Stakes: Anni Albers's imminent consecration, just as Rauschenberg arrives at the college

Fuller takes Larsen up in a small plane; she photographs from the air his collapsed geodesic dome, lying flat. Atmosphere: An aerial view, domes and spheres spread out below; a mixture of humor and experimental daring Stakes: Failure turned into an iconic image

After weeks of assembling venetian-blind strips, the crew makes the final connection; the dome was supposed to rise — it does not budge. Atmosphere: Expectation, then defeat; the nickname “Supine Dome” as an ironic epitaph Stakes: Failure at the heart of experimental teaching

During the summer session, at one of Fuller's demonstrations, he holds up a solid, announcing their old friend the tetrahedron; Elaine later declares that she fell in love with Bucky at that very moment. Words: “And here's our old friend, the tetrahedron”. Atmosphere: Fascination mixed with humor. Stakes: Fuller's charisma over the community.
Stakes: The documented failure of the first geodesic dome: the structure stays lying down (the “Supine Dome”), with Elaine de Kooning posing valiantly in the photos.

Cage knows he is entering the lions' den. He opens with an ironic portrait of the neurotic artist running to the psychoanalyst, rebuilds music from scratch, hands out his provocations (neoclassicism against nature, Schoenberg and Stravinsky overrated, materialist tonal harmony), then lets fly: Beethoven was in error — a barb aimed at Bodky, who is teaching the late quartets — before concluding with an Eastern benediction. Words: “Beethoven was in error”; good music guides the good life Atmosphere: overheated, polemical; the author describes the BMC milieu as fiery, intimate, endless in its quarrels Stakes: An unknown composer challenges the European musical establishment before its most eminent local representative

During the summer institute, Fuller tries to raise his first geodesic dome in aluminum; Albers, at the same time, makes his first engraving on Vinylite plastic. Atmosphere: A building site of experiment, industrial materials amid the mountains Stakes: The meeting of two utopias of modern material

In love with his medium, he paints with his hands, his palms, his fists; for every spot of pigment on the worn Oriental rug, they put down a dab of fresh paint to placate the concierge Words: They each agreed that the other was the worst artist in the class Atmosphere: the physical joy of matter, complicity, small domestic smuggling Stakes: intuitive freedom before the quest for discipline
